title: Climate change favours large seasonal loss of Arctic ozone
abstract: Abstract Chemical loss of Arctic ozone due to anthropogenic halogens is driven by temperature, with more loss occurring during cold winters favourable for formation of polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs). We show that a positive, statistically significant rise in the local maxima of PSC formation potential (PFP LM ) for cold winters is apparent in meteorological data collected over the past half century. Output from numerous General Circulation Models (GCMs) also exhibits positive trends in PFP LM over 1950 to 2100, with highest values occurring at end of century, for simulations driven by a large rise in the radiative forcing of climate from greenhouse gases (GHGs). We combine projections of stratospheric halogen loading and humidity with GCM-based forecasts of temperature to suggest that conditions favourable for large, seasonal loss of Arctic column O 3 could persist or even worsen until the end of this century, if future abundances of GHGs continue to steeply rise.
problem: The expected recovery of the Arctic ozone layer from reduced halogen emissions is challenged by climate change, as rising greenhouse gases cool the stratosphere and create more favorable conditions for the chemical reactions that destroy ozone.
method: We propose an Iterative Selection Approach to detect trends in the local maxima of PSC formation potential from meteorological and climate model data, combining these forecasts with halogen and humidity projections to evaluate future chemical loss of Arctic ozone.
task: The task is to project the future evolution of seasonal Arctic ozone loss until the end of the century by combining General Circulation Model temperature forecasts with projections of stratospheric halogen and humidity levels under various greenhouse gas scenarios.

Descent rates are calcu- lated directly from the heating rates provided by the ERA5 reanalysis. From the two different options provided by ECMWF, we use the total (all sky) heating rates and not the clear sky heating rates. The vertical range of the model domain is 350–1900 K and the horizontal resolution is 150 km.
